title: Letters from Hill End
paragraphs: The train had been rattling north for hours, carrying Ruby and hundreds of other children out of London, away from the war. She sat squashed between two boys from her street, with her gas-mask box bumping against her knees and a brown label tied to her coat button, as if she were a parcel. That morning, on the crowded platform, Mum had hugged her so tightly that Ruby's hat had fallen off. 'Be brave, love,' Mum had said. 'It won't be for long.'

In the village hall, the evacuees were lined up against the wall while local families walked up and down, choosing. One by one, the other children were led away, until only Ruby was left, clutching her small brown suitcase. At last, a tall woman in muddy boots stepped forward. She looked Ruby up and down, the way the greengrocer back home inspected a crate of apples. 'You'll do,' said Mrs Hollis, and that was all.

Everything about Hill End Farm was bewildering. Instead of buses and barrows and the chatter of neighbours, there were cows that stared, hens that pecked and a silence so deep that Ruby could hear her own heartbeat at night. There was no electric light, only oil lamps that smelled of smoke. Mrs Hollis had run the farm alone since her son, Oscar, had joined the army, and she worked from before dawn until after dark. She could spot a stray lamb on the far side of the valley, yet she hardly seemed to notice Ruby at all, except to give curt orders: 'Shut that gate. Wipe your boots. Eat up.'

On Sunday, Ruby wrote her first letter home. 'Dear Mum,' she wrote. 'I am having a lovely time. The farm is very big and I have a bedroom all to myself. Mrs Hollis is very kind. Please don't worry about me. Love from Ruby.' She did not mention that she had cried into her pillow every night, or that she had secretly fed her boiled cabbage to the sheepdog under the table.

One grey afternoon, the postman brought a thin envelope. Mrs Hollis turned it over and over in her rough red hands, but she did not open it. Ruby noticed that her fingers were trembling. 'You read it,' Mrs Hollis said suddenly, pushing it across the table. 'My eyes aren't what they were.' So Ruby read the letter aloud. Oscar was well, he wrote. The food was dreadful, the sergeant was worse, and he missed his mother's bread more than anything in the world.

When Ruby had finished, Mrs Hollis sat motionless. Then she pressed her apron to her face, and her shoulders began to shake. For one awful moment, Ruby thought she was crying, until she realised that Mrs Hollis was laughing. 'The sergeant's worse than the food!' she said, wiping her eyes. 'That's my Oscar.' And for the first time since Ruby had arrived, Mrs Hollis looked at her and smiled properly.

After that, things began to change. Mrs Hollis showed Ruby how to slide a hand under a sitting hen without being pecked, and how to knead dough until it felt as soft as a baby's cheek. She let Ruby choose a name for the new calf. In the evenings, they sat by the stove while Ruby read Oscar's letters aloud, even though they both knew, by then, that there was nothing wrong with Mrs Hollis's eyes.

At the end of October, Ruby wrote to Mum again. 'Dear Mum,' she wrote. 'The farm smells of cows, the nights are very quiet and I still miss you every single day. But I have named the calf Clementine, I can collect the eggs without breaking any (nearly), and Mrs Hollis is teaching me to make bread. She is not very good at smiling, but she is getting better. Love from Ruby. P.S. This time, everything I have written is true.'

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 1.
Ruby has 'a brown label tied to her coat button, as if she were a parcel'.
What does the phrase 'as if she were a parcel' suggest?
Tick one.
options: Ruby is being sent away like an object, not a person.
Ruby has been given a birthday present.
Ruby has packed too many things in her suitcase.
Ruby is on her way to the post office.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 3.
Find and copy **one** word that means short and rather rude.

Look at paragraph 3.
What did the farm use for light instead of electricity?
accept: oil lamps that smelled of smoke

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 5.
Mrs Hollis says, 'My eyes aren't what they were.'
Why do you think she **really** asked Ruby to read the letter?
questions.model: I think she was frightened that the letter might bring bad news about Oscar, so she could not bear to open it herself. Her fingers were trembling, and she turned the envelope 'over and over' without opening it.
points: explaining that she was afraid of what the letter might say, e.g. that it might bring bad news about Oscar, or that she was too nervous or upset to read it herself.
Do not accept 'her eyes were weak': paragraph 7 shows that there was nothing wrong with her eyes.

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 6.
'When Ruby had finished, Mrs Hollis sat **motionless**.'
Which word is closest in meaning to **motionless**?
Tick one.
options: still
silent
puzzled
exhausted

questions.prompt:
Look at paragraph 7.
Which **two** things did Mrs Hollis teach Ruby to do?
Tick two.
options: milk a cow
slide a hand under a hen without being pecked
drive the cows to market
knead dough

questions.prompt: Using information from the text, tick one box in each row to show whether each statement is **true** or **false**.
statements: Ruby left London on a train.
Mrs Hollis was the first person to choose an evacuee.
In his letter, Oscar said that he missed his mother's bread.
Ruby named the new calf Clementine.

questions.prompt:
Which is the best summary of paragraphs 5 to 7?
Tick one.
options: Good news in a letter from Oscar helps Mrs Hollis and Ruby to become closer.
Mrs Hollis gets bad news about Oscar and sends Ruby back to London.
Ruby writes to her mum to say that she is having a lovely time.
Ruby learns to read by practising with Oscar's letters.

questions.prompt:
Compare Ruby's two letters to her mum.
Which statement best describes the difference between them?
Tick one.
options: The first letter hides how Ruby really feels, but the second letter tells the truth.
The first letter is honest, but the second letter is full of made-up stories.
In the second letter, Ruby asks her mum to take her home.
In the second letter, Ruby says that she has a bedroom all to herself.

questions.prompt:
What impressions do you get of Mrs Hollis?
Give **two** impressions, using evidence from the text to support each one.
questions.model: At first, Mrs Hollis seems cold and unfriendly: she only says 'You'll do' when she chooses Ruby, and she gives 'curt orders'. She is also very hard-working, because she runs the farm alone and works 'from before dawn until after dark'.
points: each different impression that is backed up with evidence from the text (1 mark each), such as:
unfriendly or cold at first: 'You'll do'; she gives 'curt orders'; she 'hardly seemed to notice Ruby at all'
hard-working: she ran the farm alone and 'worked from before dawn until after dark'
sharp-eyed: she 'could spot a stray lamb on the far side of the valley'
a loving, worried mother: her fingers trembled when Oscar's letter came
kind and patient later on: she teaches Ruby to knead dough and lets her name the calf

questions.prompt:
How do Ruby's feelings about living at Hill End Farm change during the story?
Explain fully, using evidence from the text.
questions.model: At first, Ruby is homesick and unhappy. Everything is 'bewildering', she 'cried into her pillow every night', and she only pretends to her mum that she is 'having a lovely time'. After Oscar's letter, Mrs Hollis becomes kinder and teaches Ruby things, so Ruby starts to feel happier and more at home. She names the calf Clementine and is learning to make bread, and her second letter is honest: 'This time, everything I have written is true.'
points: Explains that at first Ruby is unhappy, homesick or lonely, with evidence, e.g. she 'cried into her pillow every night'.
Explains that by the end Ruby feels happier or more at home, with evidence, e.g. she named the calf Clementine or is learning to make bread.
Explains why her feelings change or how her letters show it, e.g. Mrs Hollis becomes kinder after Oscar's letter, or her second letter is honest.

questions.prompt:
At the end of the story, Ruby writes that Mrs Hollis 'is not very good at smiling, but she is getting better'.
What do you think will happen between Ruby and Mrs Hollis after the story ends?
Use evidence from the text to support your prediction.
questions.model: I think they will become even closer, and Mrs Hollis will smile more and more. She is already 'getting better' at smiling, she is teaching Ruby to make bread and she let Ruby name the calf. They will probably keep reading Oscar's letters together by the stove in the evenings.
points: a sensible prediction (1 mark), e.g. they will become closer or good friends; Mrs Hollis will smile more; Ruby will learn more about the farm; they will be sad to say goodbye when Ruby goes home.

evidence from the text that supports the prediction (1 mark), e.g. Mrs Hollis is 'getting better' at smiling; she is teaching Ruby to make bread; she let Ruby name the calf Clementine; they sit by the stove reading Oscar's letters together.

questions.prompt: Number these events 1 to 5 in the order they happen in the story.
items: Mrs Hollis chooses Ruby in the village hall.
Ruby writes that everything in her letter is true.
Mum hugs Ruby on the platform.
Ruby writes that Mrs Hollis is very kind.
